query: Identify a processing route and property optimization strategy for a lightweight, multi-principal element alloy system. The goal is to achieve high density and hardness while ensuring resistance to high-temperature oxidation and aqueous corrosion. Request a hypothesis for the material composition and processing method, supporting evidence on phase stability, boundary conditions for the processing temperature, and a falsification experiment to test the mechanism of property enhancement.

generation.hypothesis: A lightweight multi-principal element alloy system based on CoCrFeNiTi processed via mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200-1300°C will achieve high density and hardness while maintaining resistance to high-temperature oxidation and aqueous corrosion through the formation of a stable dual-phase (FCC+BCC) microstructure with nanocrystalline grain refinement and protective oxide layer formation.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental powders of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti in equimolar ratios
generation.intervention: Mechanical alloying to produce nanocrystalline powder followed by spark plasma sintering at 1200-1300°C for 10 minutes under vacuum
generation.conditions: Processing temperature: 1200-1300°C, sintering time: 10 min, atmosphere: vacuum or inert gas; Service temperature: up to 650°C; Corrosion environment: aqueous solutions and molten salts
generation.structural_mediator: Dual-phase microstructure consisting of 83% FCC and 17% BCC phases with nanocrystalline grain size (<48 nm) and coherent precipitates
generation.mechanism: Synergistic effects of mechanical alloying and SPS enable precise control of phase stability, grain refinement, and precipitation hardening. The FCC phase provides ductility while BCC phase contributes to hardness. Protective oxide layers (Cr2O3, Al2O3) form on the surface during high-temperature exposure, preventing further oxidation and corrosion through self-healing mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: Vickers hardness >650 Hv, compressive strength >1800 MPa, density ~7.5 g/cm³, oxidation resistance with mass gain <0.5 mg/cm² after 100h at 650°C, and corrosion rate <2 mm/year in aqueous and molten salt environments
generation.baseline: Conventional refractory high-entropy alloys (e.g., CrMoNbWV) with density ~10.55 g/cm³ and lower corrosion resistance
generation.boundary: Processing temperature must not exceed 1400°C to avoid excessive grain coarsening and Laves phase formation; alloy composition must maintain equimolar ratios to preserve high-entropy effects
generation.uncertainty: Long-term stability of the dual-phase microstructure at temperatures above 700°C; potential for selective dissolution of BCC phase in aggressive corrosive environments; variability in oxide layer formation depending on exact processing parameters
generation.falsification_experiment: Process CoCrFeNiTi alloy via SPS at 1400°C and compare microstructure, hardness, and corrosion resistance with samples processed at 1200°C. Expected falsification: If samples processed at 1400°C show significant grain coarsening, reduced hardness (<500 Hv), and increased corrosion rates (>5 mm/year), the hypothesis that optimal processing occurs at 1200-1300°C is falsified.

The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
